questions.question: For $\max Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ subject to $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, an optimal simplex tableau with basis $\mathcal{B}^*$ is known. One objective coefficient changes to $c_j'=c_j+\delta$, all other data fixed. Which parts of this tableau can change?
options: The right-hand-side column $\boldsymbol{B}^{-1}\boldsymbol{b}$, so feasibility of $\mathcal{B}^*$ must be rechecked.
The basis matrix $\boldsymbol{B}$, since $\boldsymbol{c}_{\mathcal{B}}$ changes when $x_j$ is basic.
Only the objective row; the rows $\boldsymbol{B}^{-1}\boldsymbol{A}$ and $\boldsymbol{B}^{-1}\boldsymbol{b}$ stay as they are.
Nothing at all, as long as $\delta$ stays inside the range of $c_j$.

questions.question: For $\max Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$, an optimal tableau has reduced costs $\bar{c}_k=-c_k+\boldsymbol{c}_{\mathcal{B}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{B}^{-1}\boldsymbol{A}_k$ (objective-row entries, all $\geq0$). The coefficient of a nonbasic variable $x_j$ changes to $c_j+\delta$. How does the objective row change?
options: Only $\bar{c}_j$ changes, and it becomes $\bar{c}_j-\delta$.
Only $\bar{c}_j$ changes, and it becomes $\bar{c}_j+\delta$.
Every nonbasic $\bar{c}_k$ changes by $\delta$ times an entry of $\boldsymbol{B}^{-1}\boldsymbol{A}$.
Nothing changes, because $c_j$ does not occur in $\boldsymbol{c}_{\mathcal{B}}$.

questions.question: For $\max Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ subject to $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$ with optimal basis $\mathcal{B}^*$ and optimal solution $\boldsymbol{x}^*$, one coefficient changes to $c_j'=c_j+\delta$ with $\delta$ strictly inside its range, so $\mathcal{B}^*$ stays optimal. What happens to the optimal solution?
options: Its basic part $\boldsymbol{B}^{-1}\boldsymbol{b}$ moves linearly in $\delta$, while the basis stays $\mathcal{B}^*$.
It stays $\boldsymbol{x}^*$, since $\boldsymbol{B}^{-1}\boldsymbol{b}$ does not involve $\boldsymbol{c}$.
It stays feasible, but it stays optimal only when $x_j$ is nonbasic.
It slides along an edge of the feasible region as the objective line turns.

questions.question: In an optimal tableau of $\max Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$, the basic variable $x_j$ stands in row $r$; for nonbasic $k$ let $a_{rk}=(\boldsymbol{B}^{-1}\boldsymbol{A})_{r,k}$, and let $\bar{c}_k\geq0$ be its reduced cost (objective-row entry). With $c_j'=c_j+\delta$, what does a column $k$ with $a_{rk}<0$ contribute to the range of $\delta$?
options: A lower bound $\delta\geq-\bar{c}_k/a_{rk}$
No condition, since only positive entries restrict $\delta$
An upper bound $\delta\leq\bar{c}_k/a_{rk}$
An upper bound $\delta\leq-\bar{c}_k/a_{rk}$

questions.question: In an optimal tableau of $\max Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ with reduced costs $\bar{c}_k=-c_k+\boldsymbol{c}_{\mathcal{B}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{B}^{-1}\boldsymbol{A}_k$, the variable $x_j$ is basic in row $r$, and $c_j$ changes to $c_j+\delta$. Which reduced costs change?
options: Only $\bar{c}_j$, which becomes $\bar{c}_j-\delta$, as for any single coefficient.
All of them, the basic ones included, by $\delta$ times their entry in row $r$.
Only the nonbasic ones, each by $\delta$ times its entry in row $r$ of $\boldsymbol{B}^{-1}\boldsymbol{A}$.
None, since $\boldsymbol{B}^{-1}\boldsymbol{A}$ is unchanged; only $Z^*$ moves.

questions.question: For $\max Z=4x_1+x_2+5x_3$ subject to $x_1+2x_2\leq14$, $x_2+3x_3\leq16$, $x_1+2x_3\leq10$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$ (slack variables $s_1,s_2,s_3$), the optimal tableau has basis $(x_1,x_2,s_2)$, $\boldsymbol{x}^*=(10,2,0)$, reduced cost $\bar{c}_3=2$ and column $(2,-1,4)$ of $x_3$ in $\boldsymbol{B}^{-1}\boldsymbol{A}$. For which $c_3$ does this basis stay optimal?
options: $c_3\geq3$
$c_3\leq7$
$3\leq c_3\leq7$
$c_3\leq2$

questions.question: For $\max Z=5x_1+3x_2+3x_3$ subject to $2x_3\leq14$, $2x_1+x_2+x_3\leq14$, $2x_1+2x_2+3x_3\leq19$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, the optimum is $\boldsymbol{x}^*=(\tfrac{9}{2},5,0)$ with $Z^*=\tfrac{75}{2}$, and its basis stays optimal for $\tfrac{11}{4}\leq c_2\leq5$. If $c_2$ is raised from $3$ to $4$, what is the new optimal value?

For $\max Z=2x_1+5x_2+3x_3$ subject to $3x_1+x_3\leq18$, $3x_1+2x_2+x_3\leq10$, $x_1+2x_2+2x_3\leq15$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, the optimum is $(0,\tfrac{5}{2},5)$, and an OR Modelling (Excel) report gives $x_1$ the reduced cost $-\tfrac{9}{2}$. With $\bar{c}_1=-c_1+\boldsymbol{c}_{\mathcal{B}}^{\top}\boldsymbol{B}^{-1}\boldsymbol{A}_1$, which statement is correct?
options: $\bar{c}_1=\tfrac{9}{2}$, and the basis stays optimal for $c_1\leq\tfrac{13}{2}$
$\bar{c}_1=-\tfrac{9}{2}$, and the basis stays optimal for $c_1\leq-\tfrac{5}{2}$
$\bar{c}_1=\tfrac{9}{2}$, and the basis stays optimal for $c_1\leq\tfrac{9}{2}$
$\bar{c}_1=-\tfrac{9}{2}$, so this basis is not optimal for the current $c_1=2$

questions.question: For $\max Z=5x_1+4x_2$ subject to $x_1+x_2\leq6$, $2x_1+x_2\leq10$, $x_2\leq5$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, the optimal tableau has basis $(x_1,x_2,s_3)$, nonbasic slack variables $s_1,s_2$ with reduced costs $3,1$, and the row of $x_1$ has entries $-1,1$ under $s_1,s_2$. For which $c_1$ does this basis stay optimal?
options: $c_1\geq4$
$2\leq c_1\leq6$
$4\leq c_1\leq8$
$-1\leq c_1\leq3$

questions.question: For $\max Z=c_1x_1+3x_2$ subject to $2x_1+x_2\leq10$, $x_1+3x_2\leq15$, $x_1\leq4$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, with $c_1=2$ the optimal corner is $(3,4)$, where the first two constraints are binding. Comparing the slope of the objective line with the slopes of these two constraints, for which $c_1$ does $(3,4)$ stay optimal?
options: $\tfrac{3}{2}\leq c_1\leq9$
$1\leq c_1\leq6$
$\tfrac{1}{3}\leq c_1\leq2$
$c_1\geq1$

questions.question: For a two-variable program $\max Z=c_1x_1+c_2x_2$ with $c_2>0$, a bounded feasible region and a nondegenerate optimal corner $\boldsymbol{x}^*$ where exactly two constraints are binding, $c_1$ is moved to an endpoint of its range, with $c_2$ fixed. Which statement about this endpoint is correct?
options: $\boldsymbol{x}^*$ is no longer optimal; only the neighbouring corner along that edge is.
The feasible region is cut back to the edge through $\boldsymbol{x}^*$, making that corner degenerate.
A nonbasic reduced cost has become negative, so the simplex algorithm must pivot.
The objective line is parallel to a binding constraint, and that whole edge, $\boldsymbol{x}^*$ included, is optimal.

questions.question: For $\max Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ subject to $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, the coefficient $c_j$ is moved just beyond the range in which the optimal basis $\mathcal{B}^*$ stays optimal, all other data fixed. How can one continue from the old optimal tableau?
options: Recompute the objective row; a reduced cost is negative but $\boldsymbol{B}^{-1}\boldsymbol{b}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, so simplex pivots continue from it.
$\boldsymbol{B}^{-1}\boldsymbol{b}$ now has a negative entry, so a feasible basis must be found anew, for instance with the big-M method.
The basis stays optimal but $\boldsymbol{x}^*$ shifts, so only the right-hand-side column needs to be recomputed.
A negative reduced cost means that the program is now unbounded, so there is no new optimum to find.

questions.question: For $\max Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ with an optimal basis $\mathcal{B}^*$, consider the set of all $\delta\in\mathbb{R}$ for which $\mathcal{B}^*$ stays optimal when $c_j$ is replaced by $c_j+\delta$, all other data fixed. Which description of this set is correct in general?
options: An open interval around $0$, since at its endpoints some reduced cost equals $0$
A bounded closed interval, since each nonbasic column gives an upper and a lower bound
A closed interval containing $0$, possibly unbounded or equal to $\{0\}$
A closed interval that may fail to contain $0$ when $\boldsymbol{x}^*$ is degenerate

questions.question: For $\max Z=4x_1+x_2+6x_3$ subject to $x_1+2x_3\leq10$, $x_1+x_3\leq9$, $x_1+2x_2+x_3\leq17$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, the optimal tableau has basis $(x_1,x_2,x_3)$, nonbasic slack variables $s_1,s_2,s_3$ with reduced costs $2,\tfrac{3}{2},\tfrac{1}{2}$, and the row of $x_1$ has entries $-1,2,0$ under them. How far can $c_1$ be lowered and raised with this basis staying optimal?
options: Lowered by $\tfrac{3}{4}$, raised by $\tfrac{3}{4}$
Lowered by $\tfrac{3}{4}$, raised by $\tfrac{1}{2}$
Lowered by $2$, raised by $\tfrac{3}{4}$
Lowered by $\tfrac{3}{4}$, raised by $2$

questions.question: For $\max Z=3x_1+4x_2+2x_3$ subject to $x_1+2x_2+x_3\leq10$, $2x_1+x_2+3x_3\leq15$, $x_1+x_2+x_3\leq7$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$ (slack variables $s_i$), the optimal tableau has basis $(x_1,x_2,s_2)$, nonbasic $x_3,s_1,s_3$ with reduced costs $1,1,2$ (objective-row entries), and row of $x_1$ with entries $1,-1,2$ there. If $c_1$ is raised to $5$, which variable should enter?
options: $s_3$, whose reduced cost becomes $-2$
$s_1$, whose reduced cost becomes $-1$
$x_1$, whose reduced cost becomes $-2$
None, since the reduced costs $1,1,2$ do not involve $c_1$

questions.question: For $\max Z=3x_1+4x_2+2x_3$ subject to $x_1+2x_2+x_3\leq10$, $2x_1+x_2+3x_3\leq15$, $x_1+x_2+x_3\leq7$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, the optimal basis is $(x_1,x_2,s_2)$; the slack variables $s_1,s_2,s_3$ have reduced costs $1,0,2$, and the row of $x_2$ has entries $1,0,-1$ under them. If $c_2$ rises from $4$ to $5$ (inside its range), what is the optimal dual solution $\boldsymbol{y}$?
options: $\boldsymbol{y}=(2,0,1)$
$\boldsymbol{y}=(1,0,2)$
$\boldsymbol{y}=(0,0,3)$
$\boldsymbol{y}=(\tfrac{5}{4},0,\tfrac{5}{2})$

questions.question: For $\max Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ subject to $\boldsymbol{A}\boldsymbol{x}\leq\boldsymbol{b}$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, an optimal tableau has a basic variable $x_j$ with value $x_j^*=0$, so the basic solution is degenerate. The coefficient $c_j$ changes to $c_j+\delta$. Which statement about the range of $\delta$ for this basis is correct?
options: It is $\delta\leq\bar{c}_j=0$, as for a nonbasic variable, since $x_j^*=0$.
It is all of $\mathbb{R}$, since a variable equal to $0$ adds nothing to $Z$.
Inside it $Z^*$ changes by $\delta$, since $x_j$ is a basic variable.
It comes from the row of $x_j$, may be bounded, and keeps $Z^*$ fixed.

questions.question: For $\max Z=\boldsymbol{c}^{\top}\boldsymbol{x}$ with optimal basis $\mathcal{B}^*$ and a basic variable with $x_j^*>0$, a student argues: raising $c_j$ by $\delta>0$ raises the value of $\boldsymbol{x}^*$ by $x_j^*\delta$, so $\mathcal{B}^*$ stays optimal for every $\delta\geq0$. What is wrong with this argument?
options: Nothing: the range of a basic coefficient is never bounded above.
Raising $c_j$ changes $\boldsymbol{B}^{-1}\boldsymbol{b}$, so $\boldsymbol{x}^*$ may become infeasible.
A feasible point with larger $x_j$ gains more than $x_j^*\delta$ and can overtake $\boldsymbol{x}^*$.
It fails only when $\boldsymbol{x}^*$ is degenerate; otherwise it is correct.

questions.question: For $\max Z=2x_1+5x_2+c_3x_3$ subject to $3x_1+x_3\leq18$, $3x_1+2x_2+x_3\leq10$, $x_1+2x_2+2x_3\leq15$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$, with $c_3=3$ the optimum is $(0,\tfrac{5}{2},5)$, and its basis stays optimal exactly for $\tfrac{5}{2}\leq c_3\leq5$. At $c_3=5$, which other corner point is also optimal, and with which value?
options: None; $(0,\tfrac{5}{2},5)$ is the only optimum, with $Z^*=\tfrac{75}{2}$

questions.question: For $\max Z=c_1x_1+2x_2$ subject to $x_1\leq3$, $x_2\leq2$, $x_1+x_2\leq5$, $\boldsymbol{x}\geq\boldsymbol{0}$ (slack variables $s_1,s_2,s_3$), with $c_1=3$ an optimal tableau has basis $(x_1,x_2,s_2)$ with $s_2=0$, nonbasic $s_1,s_3$ with reduced costs $1,2$, and row of $x_1$ with entries $1,0$ there. If $c_1$ is lowered to $1$, which statement is correct?
options: This basis is no longer optimal, yet $(3,2)$ is still optimal, with $Z^*=7$.
This basis stays optimal, since $(3,2)$ is optimal for every $c_1\geq0$.
This basis is no longer optimal, so the optimum moves to $(0,2)$, with $Z^*=4$.
This basis stays optimal, since lowering $c_1$ never makes a reduced cost negative.
